articles.title: The Call for Working-Class Liberalism Is Coming From Inside the House
articles.author: Gerard Di Trolio
articles.content: The socialist left has a vexed relationship with major economists. This is a problem, because it sometimes leaves the Left on the outside of contemporary economic debates. Daron Acemoglu is precisely the sort of economist that the Left should not ignore. Alongside his frequent collaborators Simon Johnson and James A. Robinson, he is a 2024 Nobel laureate in economics. He is also among the world’s most cited economists. His new book, What Happened to Liberal Democracy? , has already received lot of attention, as his recent spat with The Economist shows. Acemoglu’s work can be summed up in the proposition that institutions matter for economic growth. He identifies two types of institutions. Inclusive political and economic institutions constrain power, protect rights, and broaden access to opportunity, encouraging investment and innovation. Extractive institutions concentrate wealth and authority in a few hands, shutting out most people from political and economic participation. Extractive institutions may generate growth in the short term, but tend to undermine long-term prosperity. In What Happened to Liberal Democracy? , Acemoglu argues that technological innovation does not automatically produce shared prosperity. Who benefits depends on who controls technology, and how political and economic institutions distribute its gains. This perspective is unlikely to elicit many objections from Jacobin readers. Indeed, the Left’s interest in institutions long predates Acemoglu and Johnson’s intervention. From Nicos Poulantzas and the Analytical Marxists to more recent work by Stephen Maher and Scott Aquanno, Marxists have developed considered accounts of how institutions both reflect and shape struggles among classes and social forces. But Acemoglu’s new book is a useful reminder that these questions remain central, and its argument deserves engagement from the Left. Clearly, the idea that institutions matter is not controversial. But what deserves closer scrutiny is the question of how institutions are made, whose power they entrench, and whether they can be remade. Acemoglu is not without his critics beyond the classical liberals at The Economist . Adam Tooze has argued that Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson have a Whiggish approach to history that puts liberal democracy at the center. Economists like Mushtaq Khan have challenged them on placing such a high premium on the importance of Western-style property rights to set the stage for economic growth. The greatest challenge to this framework is the specter of China. Acemoglu’s account of inclusive and extractive institutions can explain underdevelopment caused by colonial institutions in Africa and Latin America . It has a much harder time explaining China’s rise. Authoritarian institutions may help explain China’s phase of export-led industrialization, like they did South Korea and Taiwan in the 1970s. But it seems less able to explain how the country now pushes the technological frontier in a number of industries. Acemoglu associates high-tech innovation with inclusive institutions that allow for entrepreneurialism, entry of new firms, open debate and research, and patents that protect innovators from confiscation. Not Your Dad’s Bourgeois Institutions The Left has an uneven history when it comes to institutional theory. Some Marxists have, for the most part, treated institutions as instruments of bourgeois rule, drawing on the The Communist Manifesto ’s characterization of the state as a “committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie.” This has encouraged a structural functionalism in which institutions are understood primarily to stabilize and help reproduce capitalism. In fairness, several Marxist theorists have pushed beyond this view. Poulantzas argued that the state was the “material condensation” of the balance of class forces in his 1978 book, State, Power, Socialism , while the Analytical Marxists pursued lines of inquiry that were unabashedly outside Marxist orthodoxy, particularly in their treatment of institutional questions. More recently, Stephen Maher and Scott M. Aquanno have theorized what they call Institutional Marxism (IM). Informed by the work of Leo Panitch and Sam Gindin, the IM perspective argues that state, business, and working-class institutions are shaped by the struggles among social forces and, in turn, give each period of capitalism its distinctive form. This lineage has included some heavy-hitting interventions. Famed development economist and September Group member Pranab Bardhan’s analysis shows how states can tolerate inefficient economic institutions when particular elite fractions capture them, while Vivek Chibber emphasizes that industrial policy cannot succeed without proper design. In this context, What Happened to Liberal Democracy? makes a number of arguments that the Left will nod its head along with and others it will vigorously dispute. The Left will agree that, in many liberal democratic countries, the working class has been left behind, social bonds have frayed, and artificial intelligence (AI), if handled poorly, is a threat to rebuilding a prosperous society. More controversial is his call for a “working-class liberalism” and the political project it entails. Acemoglu starts off by laying out what he believes constitute the great successes of liberal democracies. This is where the Whiggish tendency Tooze identifies becomes glaring. Acemoglu genuinely believes in the promise of liberal democracy, especially compared with its actually existing alternatives. However, it would be unfair to call his account purely Whiggish. Acemoglu frames liberal democracy as an incomplete but essentially progressive project, the failures of which can be cured by recuperating its fundamental commitments. He acknowledges liberalism’s historical failures, such as colonialism and lack of rights for women, but also believes that its successes have contributed to its present malaise. For Acemoglu, this malaise includes the de-linking of wages from productivity. He places greater blame for this on technology than on the declining power of organized labor. He also underscores the growing cultural and educational divide between the working class and what might, though he does not use the term, be called the professional-managerial class (PMC). Culture War in the Digital Age Acemoglu believes that educated liberals’ efforts at social engineering across a range of cultural issues have exacerbated this divide and have led to a working-class backlash. Algorithms and AI aggravate these problems. A staunch defender of free speech, Acemoglu puts forward a novel proposal — regulate the algorithms, not the speech. This would mean social media feeds would show users content from the accounts they follow rather than shepherding them toward the latest outrage or viral post. On the AI front, Acemoglu is adamant about creating what he calls “ pro-worker AI .” Pro-worker AI would help workers perform existing tasks more effectively, acquire new capabilities, and take on entirely new tasks. Any given job is a collection of tasks. AI can either automate many of those tasks or enhance the productivity of the humans that perform them. Acemoglu believes that the current business model and ideological orientation of AI companies give them no incentives to develop pro-worker AI. For him, the future direction of AI is therefore a test of liberal democracy. Responding to AI will require not only state regulation but also public deliberation in the best liberal-democratic tradition. Acemoglu rightly grasps that AI is not going anywhere. Donald Trump could throw Sam Altman and Dario Amodei in prison tomorrow and dissolve their companies, and AI would still persist, if perhaps at a slower pace. The rest of Acemoglu’s vision for working-class liberalism seeks to reconnect liberal democracy with workers’ material interests, social prestige, and political power, especially for those without university degrees. He makes it clear that he values traditional liberal principles of pluralism, freedom of expression, the rule of law, and democratic self-government. But he wants liberalism to prioritize good jobs, rising wages, public services, worker voice, and broadly shared technological progress. Such an agenda would not be out of place at a rally hosted by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez or Bernie Sanders. A more fraught matter for the Left is Acemoglu’s view that working-class liberalism should empower local communities and accommodate diverse values and opinions, within the bounds of basic liberties, rather than imposing cultural change from above. It raises the contentious question of the extent to which the consent and solidarity of the broader working-class majority can be secured when the terms of cultural politics are shaped without broad democratic participation. The Limits of Working-Class Liberalism Acemoglu insists that skepticism toward social engineering from above must not mean compromising minorities’ civil rights. He points to the example of Ireland’s citizens assemblies , which helped clear the way for the referenda legalizing same-sex marriage and repealing the constitutional ban on abortion, as proof that deliberation among the public in a liberal democracy can produce progressive wins. After its early appearance, the idea of citizens’ assemblies largely disappears from the rest of the book. For all of his enthusiasm for returning to liberal democracy’s local deliberative traditions, there is no extended engagement with the idea of citizens’ assemblies or other ways of enriching local democracy, such as participatory budgeting . This is the problem with much of the literature that seeks to defend liberal values. It offers little vision as to how democracy itself might be deepened beyond making sure existing political institutions start working properly again. Local deliberation is necessary, but it has its limits given the other issues that Acemoglu wants governments to address. As the Center for Working Class Politics’s Dustin Guastella notes , Acemoglu’s working-class liberalism often overlooks the fact that: To deliver broad based prosperity we need to solve major economic puzzles including trade, finance, labor migration, tech displacement, industrial policy, and public debt. None of these issues can be dealt with at the local level. Local deliberation may determine whether a community accepts an AI data center, but it cannot determine overall AI policy. Nor can it develop trade policy. Those kinds of interventions require a central government. The Institution of War Acemoglu also makes the common mistake of making American liberalism and social democracy interchangeable. He supports both New Deal liberalism and European social democracy. In the United States, organized labor was treated as a special interest within the New Deal coalition, whereas in European social democracies, it was a foundational political force. Failing to distinguish between the two leads to a much weaker understanding as to why the United States is an outlier among advanced economies, with its leaner welfare state and higher inequality. There are other notable omissions. Given the book’s concern with the trajectories of liberalism and social democracy, as well as challenges facing liberal democracies, its exclusion of Adam Przeworski is surprising. Przeworski has argued that there is not systemic collapse of democracy around the world, only political frictions resulting from localized institutional instability. Another surprising absence is mention of Amartya Sen. Sen’s capability approach overlaps with Acemoglu’s working-class liberalism in terms of concern with improving workers’ capabilities and promoting bottom-up democratic deliberation to better understand what communities need. The most conspicuous absence, however, is foreign policy. If liberal democracy is under threat in the United States from Donald Trump and declining faith in institutions, these developments cannot be separated from foreign policy. While the Great Recession is often tied to much of America’s current malaise, 9/11, the war on terror and the invasion of Iraq have also shaped our current moment. Spencer Ackerman has persuasively written about how those events led to Trump’s presidency. The lies that led to Iraq and the twenty-year occupation of Afghanistan were bound to corrode faith in government trust. Trump’s dovish act was always a fraud, but it played a major role in his electoral success. The Missing Agent of Change In the 2020s, American democracy is once again threatened by its foreign policy, this time over the genocide in Gaza. Freedom of speech and the right to protest have come under increasing strain . In the same way that the war on terror generated a broader malaise and skepticism toward institutions that contributed to the current situation, the suppression of free speech about the Gaza genocide — and successive Democratic and Republican administrations readiness to allow Israel to act with impunity — will further weaken American democracy over the long term. Foreign policy is by far the book’s largest omission. A further problem is that the book fails to map out exactly how working-class liberalism will come about. When discussing changing mores in society, Acemoglu points to things like civil rights, women entering the workforce, and gay marriage. Yet he offers little analysis of how social movements undergirded these advances. Although the book is a political manifesto, it is hard to understand if it is aimed at building a movement for working-class liberalism or a plea to liberal elites to do better. One of Acemoglu’s most curious statements comes not from the book but from an interview he gave while promoting it. In an interview posted on Bardhan’s Substack, Acemoglu states: I believe that the cause of labor has been significantly damaged by communist and ideological unions, because they have stuck to the ultimately self-destructive policy of working for international aims rather than for the betterment of their members, and in the process they have alienated management. So, in my mind we need a new kind of business unionism. There is a lot to unpack here. Communist-run unions in liberal democracies certainly hurt themselves by following Moscow’s zigzags, though state repression also played a role in their decline in the United States. At the same time, as Judith Stepan-Norris and Maurice Zeitlin have shown in their seminal Left Out: Reds and America’s Industrial Unions , communist-led unions in the 1930s and ’40s did more for racial and gender equality than other union leaderships and had more democratic union constitutions. These are basic values that everyone expects unions to have today, but they were certainly not universal back then. International commitments, moreover, have always been part of the labor movement, even when they were internally contested. Among these commitments, the labor movement can count support for the Republicans in the Spanish Civil War and for the anti-apartheid movement as well as opposition to US intervention in Central America. Today unions are taking a critical stand toward Israel. Acemoglu invokes the hard-hat-versus-hippie divide during the Vietnam War, but, as Penny Lewis has shown in Hardhats, Hippies, and Hawks , there was significant working-class opposition to the war. Acemoglu’s suspicion of union engagement with these kinds of activities actually undermines one of his key arguments: that the renewal of liberal democracy will require workers to have a voice outside the workplace. Taking Power Seriously Acemoglu identifies the decline of associational life as a major problem for liberal democracy. For working-class people, unions were once a key part of that associational world. Business unionism is a subpar foundation on which to sustain it. Unions have played a major role in democratization, notably in Brazil, South Africa, and South Korea. In an American context, the complacency of business unionism during the postwar settlement left unions unable to organize emerging sectors and vulnerable to Ronald Reagan’s attacks. Unions are bulwarks of democracy in the workplace and society, and they should engage in politics at all levels. Implicit in Acemoglu’s defense of business unionism is a concern about the division between the cultural politics of rank-and-file union members and those of a more ideological leadership. Unions can have a progressive effect on members’ attitudes, including toward cultural issues that Acemoglu might regard as divisive. However, this influence is democratic only when unions ensure space for internal disagreement. In order to not blur the line between associational democracy and top-down social engineering, dissent cannot be stigmatized, and open deliberation is essential. These reservations, however, do not obscure what the Left can take from Acemoglu’s book. His book deserves serious engagement. He identifies several realities that the Left cannot escape from: economic growth remains essential to improving the lot of the working class, at least in the medium term; control of technology is up for grabs; and that many working people feel deeply alienated. As the Left gets serious about building economic and political institutions, understanding the trade-offs in institutional design will be crucial. Acemoglu’s work and the economic role of institutions cannot be ignored.

articles.title: Tech Authoritarian Doomsayers
articles.content: In June 2024 , investor David Sacks hosted a high-dollar fundraiser for then presidential candidate Donald Trump at his Pacific Heights mansion in San Francisco, bringing together the titans of Silicon Valley and venture capitalism to pledge their allegiance — and financial support — to the candidate promising to make their wildest tech-authoritarian dreams come true. The dinner party was orchestrated by then Ohio Sen. J.D. Vance, who served as a point of contact between Sacks and Trump, the former real estate tycoon who had notoriously been less than friendly to Big Tech during his first term. This time, however, Trump reportedly struck a different tone, criticizing Bidenera regulations on the ascendant industries of crypto and artificial intelligence (AI), promising to lift them if elected. Netting a cool $ 12 million for Trump, the event helped kick off the new era of oligarchic tech rule in Washington, D.C., that’s shaping all of our lives as a burgeoning class of billionaire elites tears down the pylons of U.S. democracy while ushering in a counterfeit world of synthetic slop meant to enrich the corporate overlords and, if necessary, bring about societal apocalypse for the rest of humanity. Not long after this fateful gathering, Trump tapped Vance — who counts billionaire tech baron Peter Thiel as his consigliere and patron — to be his vice presidential nominee. Following Trump’s election, Sacks was named as the administration’s ​ “ crypto and AI czar,” in charge of unleashing the industry at full force. Today, whatever guardrails had previously been placed on Big Tech have been effectively removed, and the CEOs that infamously sat behind Trump during his inauguration last year are now in full control of our economy — and increasingly our entire political future. The story of that Trump fundraiser is recounted in Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor’s illuminating new book End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World , wherein the authors, both revelatory thinkers and writers on the Left, explain how the inciters of our current crises are benefiting from the chaos they’ve wrought while plotting their own escape, whether via the underground or another celestial realm. In the book, Klein and Taylor define their subject of ​ “ end times fascism” as: A fascism embedded in an understanding that something immense is ending, and it responds to this discomfiting truth with accelerationist zeal. Rather than alter the human-created economic and social systems driving crisis and collapse, its progenitors insist that it is the human story itself that has hit a wall and that only a small, deserving group of humans will survive the coming cataclysm — whether in their bunkered city in the sky or their bunkered corporate city or their bunkered nation-state, fortressed against alien invaders. … It is a story rooted in that old seductive dream of the chosen few ascending to a gated paradise, while the rest of us are abandoned to the floods and fires of the damned. The purveyors of this dynamic, according to Klein and Taylor, believe that summoning a digital superintelligence through AI justifies abandoning environmental sustainability, so long as they are in turn handed the reins to decision-making power over an unruly public that might have other ideas about how to arrange society. Thiel, for his part, wrote back in 2009 : ​ “ I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” The co-founder of tech giant Palantir — which contracts with the Trump administration to surveil immigrants, supports U.S. military weapons systems and aids the Israeli Defense Forces — is also deeply entrenched with Marc Andreessen, a billionaire venture capitalist with newfound purchase in the White House who believes in fully eliminating the corporate regulatory state and calls himself an ​ “ effective accelerationist” for an AI-driven destiny. These tech authoritarians didn’t come out of nowhere; rather, they’ve been incubating their plans for domination over decades, as journalist Gil Durán recounts in his new book The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy. While long perceived simply as governmentally suspicious ​ “ libertarians,” Durán explains that, in fact, the class of Silicon Valley extremists to which Thiel and Andreessen belong aims to take the reins of governmental power to serve their own ends, a process we are seeing play out seemingly every day under the second Trump administration, from Elon Musk’s mass firing of federal workers under the former Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) to the rapid shrinking of government agencies. As Durán writes: Tech fascism bundles powerful technologies — AI, crypto, defense tech, social media platforms, surveillance systems — toward authoritarian goals. These technologies are bound together under the control of a small, interconnected group of oligarchs who, simultaneously integrated into the highest levels of government, are creating an authoritarian infrastructure with boundless power. Its goal, like MAGA’s, is to privatize the public and eliminate democracy. Not content with sporting the full backing of Trump and his allies, this hyper-rich doomsayer set is splurging to make sure their party goes unspoiled after the November midterm elections. The Silicon Valley firm Andreessen Horowitz (yes, co-run by that Marc Andreessen) has already spent more than $ 115 million this cycle — making it the biggest known spender this campaign season. That includes more than $ 10 million to MAGA Inc., Trump’s Super PAC, as well as many millions more to other PACs aiming to curb any oversight of AI or cryptocurrency. Thiel, meanwhile, has poured millions of dollars into defeating a billionaire wealth tax proposal in California, and millions more linked to the tech billionaire are being funneled through dark money expenditures. A completely broken campaign finance system has made this kind of interference in our political system routine. But it also speaks to a deeper reality: the public doesn’t want the future these rich losers are selling, so they’re being forced to burn parts of their fortunes to fend off any democratic control. Far from a gilded status quo pockmarked by data centers and unaffordable groceries, voters are displaying an appetite for getting behind a different vision — one where the working-class majority takes the front seat, and the tech bros and their corporate benefactors step aside. More than 70 % of Americans say that tech companies currently have too much power, and nearly the same level say they support using antitrust laws to go after them. When it comes to overseeing the development of AI, fewer than one in five U.S. residents say they trust Big Tech. Meanwhile, democratic socialists and outspoken progressives keep winning primaries, promising to materially benefit people who work for a living through enhanced social programs funded by stripping wealth away from the real parasites of society — the super rich. From Angie Nixon in Florida, a Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member who won the Democratic primary for Senate, to Donavan McKinney in Michigan, a DSA-endorsed candidate who won the primary for a Detroit U.S. House seat, voters are showing a willingness to back campaigns seeking to rearrange society fully in the interests of the working class. The end-time fascists and tech authoritarians want to scare us into believing that a catastrophic dystopia is all that can await us, so it’s best to just go along with their prophetic hypercapitalist scheme. The truth is that we all control our collective future. There’s no better time than now to make that known. _____________________ Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor, End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World , Farrar, Straus and Giroux, Sept. 2026 . articles.title: Donald Trump’s Imperialism of Decline Is a Global Menace
articles.author: Atul Kohli
articles.content: To make sense of US foreign policy under Donald Trump, we need to see it against the long-term historical background. Trump’s approach to world affairs may be erratic, but that does not mean it is completely without precedent. The United States has long been an imperial power. While not establishing formal colonies, the US has instead created an informal empire in which obsequious governments in the Global South enable the pursuit of American political and economic interests. Throughout its history, American imperialism has come in three varieties: hard militarism, covert regime change, and multilateral coercion. Trump’s brand of imperialism continues along these pathways, albeit with some significant changes, especially its brazenness. America’s Militarist Tradition Recent US intervention in Iran is part of a long American tradition of hard military imperialism that stretches back to the Philippines in the early twentieth century and notably includes Vietnam and Iraq in the post–World War II period. American goals in such cases were often grandiose but vague. In the case of the Philippines, for example, the stated goal was to establish an entrepôt to China that could be America’s version of Hong Kong. Saving Southeast Asia from communism was of course the justification for the invasion of Vietnam, while the war in Iraq was supposed to be the beginning of a mission to bring democracy to the Middle East. Hard militarism in these imperial interventions of the past seldom enabled the United States to achieve its avowed goals: the US never really gained access to the enormous Chinese market; Vietnam did go communist, but the rest of Southeast Asia was never threatened and very much remains capitalist; Iraq is now a chaotic state, and the war destabilized the entire Middle East. Meanwhile, poor countries of the world have paid a heavy price, not only in economic devastation, but especially in lives lost. For example, when the deaths of soldiers and of war-related civilians are combined, nearly half a million Filipinos died during the US-Philippines war; some three million Vietnamese died in the Vietnam War; and half a million Iraqis may have perished during George W. Bush’s preemptive war of choice. Why the United States went to war in Iran in 2026 remains a puzzle. The consensus within the American intelligence community was that Iran did not pose any immediate threat to the US. While Israel was an integral partner in the war, the suggestion that Israel pushed the United States into attacking Iran is also not persuasive; the tail does not wag the dog. American intervention in Iran was, once again, an imperial war of choice. The vague but grandiose goals included further destroying Iran’s military and nuclear capabilities (a preemptive war), access to Iranian oil (a war of greed), and liberating Iranians from a theocratic dictatorship (a quixotic war). Although the war is still unfolding, the results will probably not be all that different from those in the past. Iran and its people will have paid a heavy price in terms of lives and well-being, but the United States is not likely to achieve its grandiose goals. Profitable Failures Given this record of recurring failures, the question that remains is why the United States repeatedly treads the path of military imperialism. The sanguine answer that such wars are recurring mistakes will not do; to accept such a view, one would have to assume that there is no learning curve among America’s powerful. The genuine answer is more complicated and has both a political and an economic component. The United States possesses enormous surplus power in the world. The temptation to use this power is ever present, especially if provoked by lesser powers. As Madeline Albright, Bill Clinton’s secretary of state, famously remarked to Colin Powell, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff: “What is the point of having this superb military that you are always talking about if we cannot use it?” The readily provoked Trump does not ask such probing questions; he has already used military force against seven countries, and more may well follow. Military interventions also lead to economic benefits. Discussions of the failure to achieve avowed war goals often proceed by underlining the cost of particular wars. In the case of Trump’s latest adventure, estimates range from some $40 billion to more than $100 billion. While useful, such discussions often miss a core dynamic of imperial interventions. Taxpayers and soldiers are the ones who bear the costs of such wars, while the benefits accrue to a much more select layer. In the case of Iran, oil companies have profited handsomely: both ExxonMobil and Chevron Corporation reported record profits due to higher oil prices resulting from the war. In addition, the defense budget is likely to go up significantly because of the war, benefiting military industries. This pattern of overseas interventions providing an occasion for higher defense budgets also has a long American history; for example, during the early Cold War years, there was considerable reluctance in the United States to increase defense expenditures to the levels sought by the Truman administration. The Korean War put an end to such hesitations, and the budget skyrocketed. As Dean Acheson, Truman’s secretary of state, then crowed: “Korea came along and saved us.” Regime Change Covert capture of Venezuela’s President Nicolás Maduro is also part of a long tradition of deposing rulers in the Global South who are deemed to be antithetical to American interests and replacing them with pro-American minions. Earlier examples include Mohammad Mossadegh in Iran, Jacobo Árbenz in Guatemala, Patrice Lumumba in the Congo, and Salvador Allende in Chile. Such regime change operations have often led to significant economic gains for American corporations but also to unsavory rulers and distorted economies in poor countries. Anointed by the United States, Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi of Iran replaced the democratically elected Mossadegh, ruling autocratically, selling oil to the United States, and establishing a cozy relationship with American corporations based on the exchange of oil revenues for American goods, especially military hardware. In Guatemala, the overthrow of Árbenz enabled the United Fruit Company to recover its expropriated land and to reverse labor and land reforms, creating a classic banana republic. Lumumba’s assassination led to three decades of ruinous rule by Mobutu Sese Seko in the Congo (which he renamed Zaire) while providing an economic opening for US companies. The Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet reversed Allende’s nationalization of US companies such as Anaconda, Kennecott, ITT, and Dow Chemicals. Venezuela is very likely to follow this pattern. The removal of Maduro was clearly an effective military maneuver, but it was also an act of extreme imperial hubris. The fact that an alternate leadership was found so quickly — and without violence — appears to be a modest departure from similar covert actions of the past. But taking direct control of Venezuela’s oil revenues goes further than previous interventions in Latin America or other regions. This brash move hearkens back to an earlier phase in the history of informal empires. Britain controlled the finances of post–Opium War China and then managed the finances of Egypt in the late nineteenth century in partnership with France. The reappearance of this form of financial control in the twenty-first century marks a further erosion of previous norms of sovereignty and self-determination. As the United States eases sanctions on Venezuela and American investment returns, Venezuela’s economy is bound to grow. Much will then be said in official circles and mainstream media outlets about how much better off Venezuelans now are under American tutelage. What will be forgotten is how much American sanctions hurt Venezuela’s economy in the first place. The pattern of Venezuela’s rebound is also likely to involve a sharply unequal economy still dependent on oil exports to the United States for its erratic buoyancy. Trump was strikingly brazen in stating that the goal of this intervention was to gain access to Venezuela’s oil for American companies. Gone were all the shibboleths of saving a country from communism or promoting democracy. How does one interpret this shift? The answer could simply be the leadership team involved: Trump and his acolytes are no liberals; they believe in “might is right” and do not feel the need to cover up their rapacious actions in ideological clothing. But it is more plausible that we are seeing a growing realization at the highest echelons of the US state that America is a shrinking power. Legitimacy and soft power are resources that global hegemons value. It may well be that the United States is giving up on such ambitions and is likely to be even more dangerous in the future, because declining powers believe in taking what they can by force, consequences be damned. Forcing Doors Open This suggestion that America is a shrinking empire is consistent with the fact that its third imperial pathway, multilateral coercion, may also be in retreat. Historically, the United States has cooperated with other Western powers to subjugate countries in the global periphery. For example, it was part of an imperial condominium that divided up China in the first half of the twentieth century. As a matter of fact, the Unites States used the decline of Qing China as an occasion to promulgate the Open Door Notes, a set of propositions that became a framework for America’s preferred road to imperialism, informal empire. This would mean that poor countries could enjoy nominal sovereignty if they left their economies open for advanced capitalist countries to exploit. Following this roadmap, the United States in the post–World War II period frequently cooperated with other lesser capitalist powers like Britain and France to keep open the economies of the developing world. Most recently, the US used multilateral organizations like the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund to impose the Washington Consensus on countries in the Global South, especially in Latin America; these actions ensured that indebted American banks did not suffer financial losses. This third form of American imperialism may well now be in decline. The reasons are not hard to understand. The US economy is no longer competitive in the global arena. Free trade imperialism does not pay anymore; Trump’s tariffs and blatant imperial interventions are both indicative of this new global reality. The United States can forcibly open Latin American countries to international trade and investment, only to see China move in rather than American firms. In the political arena, too, a declining hegemon is not in a position to direct multilateral organizations to do its bidding. Nor can it readily cajole lesser powers to join imperial ventures, especially when the United States treats such powers with scorn. Notice how few takers there are as the US invites European countries to join it in opening the Strait of Hormuz. Most Americans do not think of America as an imperial country. With Trump’s overt imperialism, that form of hypocrisy is hard to sustain. Good American liberals may still take comfort in the belief that, following Trump, a well-meaning America will reemerge as a benign global hegemon. Unfortunately, that was never true in the past, and it is not likely to be so in the future.

articles.title: The Fate of the Rohingyas Is Crucial for Myanmar’s Future
articles.author: Sushovan Dhar
articles.content: In August 2024, Rohingya families gathered on the banks of the Naf River in Maungdaw, waiting to cross into Bangladesh as the fighting closed in. Drones and mortars found them there. Roughly two hundred people were killed , another entry in a catalogue of atrocity the Rohingya have been forced to keep for decades. What made this massacre different was who stood accused of it. The killing was attributed not to the Myanmar military, the army that drove three-quarters of a million Rohingya into exile in 2017, but to the Arakan Army , the ethnic Rakhine force that has spent the past two years dismantling that same military’s grip on the state. The genocidaire was in retreat but the Rohingya were dying anyway. That is the contradiction at the heart of Myanmar today, and it is why we should mark the ninth anniversary of the 2017 genocide as something other than a humanitarian remembrance. The Rohingya are usually cast as victims of a specific army and a specific campaign of expulsion. But the genocide was never only a crime committed by soldiers. It was the sharpest expression of a political order: a state built on Burman-Buddhist supremacy, a citizenship regime designed to render an entire people stateless, and a center that has always treated its ethnic peripheries as territory to be subdued rather than nations to be included. The question the anniversary poses is not whether the world remembers the Rohingya. It is whether the forces now tearing down the Myanmar state are capable of tearing down the order that produced them, or whether they will simply inherit it. Statelessness by Design The genocide was structural before it was violent. Myanmar’s postindependence state was built around a hierarchy of belonging, and the 1982 Citizenship Law codified it into a taxonomy of “national races”: 135 ethnic groups whose presence before British colonization qualified them as authentic sons of the soil. The Rohingya were left off the list. At a stroke, people who had lived in Arakan for generations were reclassified as illegal immigrants from Bengal. Statelessness was not an accident of the Rohingya condition; it was its legal foundation. This was the logic of the state itself. Independent Burma inherited from British rule a political geography in which a Burman-Buddhist core governed a ring of minority peripheries (Kachin, Shan, Karen, Chin, Rakhine). Promises of autonomy dissolved almost immediately into the reality of military domination. The relationship between center and periphery was colonial in every meaningful sense of the term: extraction, denial of self-rule, the permanent threat of force. The Tatmadaw entrenched itself as the guardian of this arrangement, a Bonapartist apparatus that governed by balancing the antagonisms beneath it while serving no interest so faithfully as its own. Burman-Buddhist chauvinism was its ideological cement, and the Rohingya were its most useful enemy: a stateless, defenseless Muslim population against whom national unity could always be manufactured. The 2017 “clearance operations” were the culmination of that logic, not a departure from it. This is the precondition for everything that follows. If the Rohingya were merely victims of one army’s brutality, the defeat of that army would be their liberation. However, if their expulsion was the work of an entire architecture — citizenship as ethnic patrimony, belonging as bloodline, the periphery as conquered territory — then the collapse of the army settles nothing. The architecture can survive the fall of any single institution that once inhabited it. It can even be rebuilt by the forces that fought the original builders. Not Democracy vs. Dictatorship That collapse is now well underway. The February 2021 coup , meant to restore untrammeled military rule, instead detonated the most serious challenge to the Myanmar state since independence. Mass protest gave way to armed resistance; People’s Defense Forces sprang up across the Burman heartland, and the established ethnic armies seized the moment to expand. Five years on, the junta controls only around a fifth of the country. It has staged sham elections and installed Min Aung Hlaing, the general behind both the genocide and the coup, as president of a nominally civilian government, while at the same time it bombs hospitals in the territories slipping from its hands. Here the internationalist left has to resist a comforting simplification. It is tempting, from a distance, to read what is happening in Myanmar as a straightforward contest between democracy and dictatorship. That story is not false, but it is dangerously incomplete. The crisis convulsing Myanmar is simultaneously a crisis of the state constructed in 1948: of Burman domination, of the unresolved claims of a dozen nationalities, of who controls territory and resources, and of what citizenship means and who is entitled to it. The war is not only about who rules the state. It is about whether that state, centralized, ethnically hierarchical, colonial toward its periphery, should exist in its present form at all. The Rohingya are the population on whom that deeper question falls most heavily, because they are the ones the existing order was most determined to exclude. Whose Self-Determination? Nowhere is the ambiguity of Myanmar’s unmaking sharper than in Rakhine, and no force embodies it more completely than the Arakan Army (AA). The AA’s rise is genuinely extraordinary. Having been founded as recently as 2009, it has seized some 90 percent of Rakhine State, captured the entire border with Bangladesh, and overrun a regional military command that had held for generations. Through its political wing, it now runs a functioning administration (courts, policing, taxation, conscription) and speaks openly of confederal self-rule. This is not banditry but state-building, animated by a real and deeply felt Rakhine nationalism, a demand for self-determination after decades of subordination to the Burman center. In its own terms, the AA is exactly what the Left says it supports: the vehicle of an oppressed nationality asserting its right to determine its future against a colonial state. And yet the territory the AA is liberating is also home to the Rohingya, and the record of how they have fared in the course of its advance is by now extensively documented. As AA forces took Buthidaung and Maungdaw in 2024, investigators recorded a familiar pattern of dispossession : villages shelled and burned, Rohingya men detained and killed, others pressed into forced labor. At Hoyyar Siri in May 2024, AA fighters are alleged to have fired on unarmed Rohingya fleeing the fighting; Human Rights Watch documented at least 170 dead, and survivors put the figure higher. Then came the killings at the Naf. Since taking control, the AA has imposed the machinery of an occupation : bans on movement and livelihood, confiscation of land, and a refusal to use the very word “Rohingya,” naming them instead as “Bengalis” or “Muslims.” Rohingya who fled AA-held areas told Amnesty International that life under the Arakan Army felt not merely as bad as life under the Tatmadaw but worse, because now they were permanently suspected of collaboration. The AA denies all of it as activist propaganda. Those denials are hard to sustain against testimony gathered by the UN’s own human rights office , Amnesty, Fortify Rights, and Human Rights Watch alike. This is the contradiction that ought to trouble anyone who thinks seriously about national liberation. The nationalism of the oppressed can harden into the domination of a new oppressor the moment it takes power. A nation defined by ethnicity and secured by territory tends to reproduce, against whatever minority lives inside its borders, the very logic of exclusion it fought to escape. The Arakan the AA is building is an Arakan for the Rakhine. It reproduces, in miniature and against the Rohingya, precisely the “national races” logic the Burman state used against the Rakhine themselves. One oppressed nationality’s road to freedom is being paved with another’s subjection. This is not a betrayal of Rakhine nationalism; rather, it is what ethnically defined self-determination looks like when it meets a population it does not count as its own. The Rohingya’s position is uniquely desperate, and the reason is structural. Every other major actor has a territory, an army, a claim. The Rohingya have none: no army that protects them, no ground they control, no patron that will fight for them. So they are caught between the armed camps and made into instruments of their own destruction. When the junta activated conscription in 2024, it forcibly recruited Rohingya men and boys, the same population it had tried to exterminate seven years earlier, to fight and die against the Arakan Army. The AA then points to the role of those fighters to justify treating the whole population as a fifth column. The victims are pressed into service, then condemned as collaborators for it. The Democratic Opposition If the Arakan Army is one horn of the dilemma, the democratic opposition is the other. Here the picture is more hopeful, though still unfinished. The change since 2017 is real. In that year, the chauvinism aimed at the Rohingya was near-total; Aung San Suu Kyi herself went to The Hague to defend the military against the charge of genocide. The coup shattered some of that consensus. Burman activists hunted by the same army began, haltingly, to recognize a kinship with the people it had hunted before them. In June 2021, the National Unity Government (NUG), the shadow administration of ousted lawmakers and resistance figures, pledged to repeal the 1982 Citizenship Law, abolish the hated verification cards, ground citizenship in birth in the country rather than membership in a “national race,” and grant international courts jurisdiction over crimes against the Rohingya. For a body dependent on a base steeped in anti-Rohingya sentiment, this took courage. But recognizing a past wrong is not the same as dismantling the structure that produced it. The NUG controls no territory in Rakhine; its writ does not run where the Rohingya live. Its citizenship reform is deferred to a future constitution that does not yet exist. The deeper problem is one that the NUG gestures at but does not resolve. So long as Myanmar’s political imagination is organized around ethnicity — around federated homelands, with each representing the patrimony of a titular nationality — the Rohingya will remain the constitutive exception, the group that fits no homeland and therefore belongs nowhere. A federation of ethnic states is a coherent answer to Burman domination. It is not by itself an answer to Rohingya statelessness. It can just as easily become a framework in which every people has its territory and the Rohingya have none. The Rohingya Are the Test This is why the Rohingya cannot be treated as a humanitarian appendix to the Myanmar conflict, a suffering to be addressed once the real political questions are settled. Their fate is the real political question posed in its most demanding form. It is the clearest available test of whether the collapse of the old order will produce a genuinely different Myanmar or merely a redistribution of territory and power among armed actors, each erecting its own machinery of belonging and unbelonging, while the deepest structures of exclusion survive the state that first built them. So far, the evidence points more toward reshuffling than transformation. The Tatmadaw is being defeated, and that is a genuine gain: an army that committed genocide is losing its capacity to commit it again. But the force supplanting it in Rakhine has begun to build an ethnic statelet that treats the Rohingya as the Burman state once treated the Rakhine. The democratic opposition has renounced the old chauvinism in words while remaining unable, and not yet fully willing, to attack its foundations. A Myanmar worthy of the name that the Spring Revolution gave it would have to break not with this or that institution but with the principle beneath all of them: the idea that belonging is a matter of ethnic descent and the nation the property of a race. It would have to found citizenship on residence and birth rather than bloodline and extend it to the Rohingya not as a concession wrung from the international community but as a right. Whether any force in Myanmar is prepared to fight for that, rather than merely for its own share of the wreckage, is the question the ninth anniversary should put to everyone who claims to stand with the country’s revolution. Nine years ago, the Myanmar state expelled the Rohingya to prove what kind of state it was. That state is now falling apart. The Rohingya are still waiting to learn whether anything different is being built in its place, or whether they are simply being handed from one guardian of the old order to the next. Their answer will tell us what the Myanmar revolution actually amounts to.

articles.title: The Rise of Germany’s Far Right Reflects a Systemic Crisis
articles.author: Gábor Scheiring
articles.content: After the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) scored 44 percent of the vote in the September 6 state election in Saxony-Anhalt, many analysts sought some single, clearly identifiable reason. The interest in the AfD’s success is well justified: what happens in Germany shapes Europe and even world politics, and most mainstream accounts seek tools with which the center can disarm the far right. In this vein, the AfD’s success is said to owe to a sluggish bureaucracy, the peculiar political culture of the former East Germany, or more simply to immigration. Yet the reliance on a single explanatory factor yields single-variable strategies in response, and such strategies are bound to fail. The rise of the far right is a symptom of a systemic crisis that has merely become more visible in eastern Germany than elsewhere. Institutions, National Character, and Subcultures One rather unconvincing group of explanations focuses on the peculiarities of national institutions. In the German case, conservative commentators often bewail a slow and frustrating bureaucracy — and it is indeed notoriously sluggish. The morning after the Saxony-Anhalt election, one of Germany’s largest news portals blamed the “sprawling bureaucratic state” for the growth of political dissatisfaction, and prescribed trimming it as the remedy. Yet such explanations share a typical flaw: they look for nationally specific factors, even though the phenomenon in question — the rise of the far right — is much more general. In each country concerned, some local particularity is blamed for such forces’ breakthroughs, whether that means the US electoral college, Britain’s first-past-the-post system, or France’s two-round presidential elections. If the causes were such unique institutional quirks, it would be hard to explain the far right’s global presence. Yet by last year, radical-right parties together formed Europe’s most popular party family, with support above the levels reached in the 1930s. In summer polling, France’s Rassemblement National stood at around 35 percent, and Britain’s Reform UK at 26. Beyond the West, Narendra Modi has governed India since 2014, and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has ruled Turkey since 2003; the former in a federal parliamentary system, the latter in a system he converted to a presidential structure. Neither institutional design has stood in their way. Simplistic cultural readings — the various decodings of the national psyche — are not much more convincing either. In Germany, this is a genre known as “Ossi-bashing” : East Germans (“Ossis”) supposedly inherited an inferior, illiberal political culture. The thesis has several eastern European variants, all of which explain the rise of illiberalism in terms of a supposedly servile national character: the homo sovieticus , the serf mentality, or civilizational incompetence. Still, in more recent years the fall of illiberal governments in Poland and Hungary has turned these same countries into international laboratories of democratic resistance. So much for the dysfunctional national psyche. As I shall explain, while eastern German particularities may explain the intensity of the AfD vote, they don’t explain the mechanism of change itself. Backlash? The cultural explanation also has a seemingly more scientific version, by now the most thoroughly refuted theory of populism, which nonetheless still organizes public debate: the cultural backlash of aging, uneducated men against unstoppable progress toward cosmopolitanism. However, the basic facts contradict this theory. The AfD was founded in 2013 by highly educated neoliberal economists led by Bernd Lucke; in the office of Bernd Baumann, the parliamentary group’s chief whip, a portrait of Friedrich Hayek hangs on the wall. The party is popular among the young: in Saxony-Anhalt, 41 percent of first-time voters ages eighteen to twenty-four voted for it . It also won 59 percent of workers , but the density of craft and small industrial businesses best predicts its strongest districts. Its financiers are frustrated big entrepreneurs: in the 2025 campaign the AfD received the largest individual donations of any party, including €1.5 million from Winfried Stöcker, founder of the diagnostics company Euroimmun. Its largest known donor is Henning Conle, a real estate billionaire who lives in Zürich and London and owns a Liechtenstein holding company. The AfD, and by extension much of today’s far right, is an exclusionary-nationalist rebranding of neoliberalism. Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party, the US Republicans, and Reform UK have traveled the same path. The far right is the party of a double revolt, of national capital and a devalued middle class. For want of anything better, a large share of workers vote for it as the only alternative to the ruling elites, even though that alternative turns out to be fake most of the time. Behind these explanations lies a common narrative: the far right is a passing disturbance in an otherwise functioning system. Chancellor Friedrich Merz, for instance, contritely “admitted” that the government does not communicate its measures well enough. If only someone could finally explain to those foolish voters how well the government is actually doing. In reality, the AfD has been growing for thirteen years, while trust in the political elite keeps falling: only 17 percent of Germans now believe the state can carry out its basic tasks . Across Western democracies, the share of people who think democracy is not important is rising. This is no longer a passing disturbance but a chronic, life-threatening illness of democracy. Firewall, Copy, Govern Misdiagnoses produce dead-end strategies. If the AfD’s rise just reflected a minoritarian subculture, then a “firewall” blocking its path might be enough to stop it. Those who imagine the AfD’s success owes to its particular policies may choose to copy them. Those who see a passing disturbance call for it to be allowed to govern, hoping it fails and ends up exposed. Yet all of these are illusory. The firewall strengthens what it is meant to wall off through three mechanisms. First, it splits the political space in two: it suggests there are five legitimate democratic parties on one side and the AfD on the other. Second, the only common denominator among the five parties is defending the establishment, so the theme of change belongs to the far right. In Germany, this is a chronic condition: as early as 1980, Chancellor Helmut Schmidt told anyone with visions to see a doctor, and this has remained the philosophy of the German center ever since, a world of small technical steps and muddling through. Third, firewall coalitions are paralyzed from birth: given the ideological contradictions between parties like the socialist Die Linke and the conservative Christian Democrats, decisive governance is impossible. Against this dithering, the plainspoken drive of the far right impresses more and more people. Co-opting the far right’s themes is another dead end. In January 2025, Friedrich Merz relied on AfD votes to pass a migration resolution in the Bundestag; at the federal election four weeks later, the AfD doubled its 2021 scores. The Danish Social Democrats invented the anti-immigration left in 2019 by adopting the far right’s migration program, yet in spring 2026 they collapsed to their worst result since 1903. The research shows the same thing : on the terrain of exclusionary nationalism, the far right is unbeatable, because voters prefer the original to the copy. The center parties increasingly resign themselves to the third option: let them govern. The idea that right-wing populism succeeds in opposition and fails in government came from the entry of the Austrian Freedom Party (FPÖ) into government in 2000: it fell from 27 percent to 10 percent in 2002. Yet in 2024 it was stronger than ever, finishing first with 29 percent. After Viktor Orbán’s sixteen years in power in Hungary, it hardly needs explaining how dangerous the belief is that the far right either fails or mellows in office. The misdiagnosis follows from how knowledge is produced. Populism research focuses ever finer methods on ever smaller variables, while the logic of clicks pushes the media toward moral panics and the personal dramas of celebrity and influencer politicians. Much of the think tank world in between the two specializes in greasing the revolving doors of power and avoids confronting elites. The systemic crisis is thus broken down into its components, even though the whole is more than the sum of its parts. Exit From Stalemate Politics is a stage, with ever more dramatic, personal, and kitschy spectacle. Yet ultimately, the fate of what’s going on in the party-political theater is decided by deeper processes. It is not particular institutions, subcultures, or groups that have fallen into crisis, but the postwar compromise that reconciled the market’s polarizing effect with democracy’s demand for equality. Two twentieth-century thinkers worked out theoretical frameworks that integrate these questions into a single system. Both wrote about the rise of fascism, but their framework fits today’s illiberalism as well. Karl Polanyi saw fascism as an exit from a stalemate. Between the two world wars, the forces of market expansion and society’s self-defense paralyzed each other; the democratic market economy became ungovernable, and in the end the elites opted to back fascism. According to Antonio Gramsci , the crisis of authority in the liberal order sets in when an economic model is exhausted, along with the institutions that temporarily reconciled capital’s need for growth with the interests of working people. Gramsci’s infamous “morbid symptoms” emerging from such an impasse are again on full display, and not only in Germany. Contemporary political economists willing to look past the firewall know this well, from Wolfgang Streeck to Nancy Fraser, but their voice is conspicuously missing from the mainstream discussion of populism. Behind the far right’s rise today also stands the exhaustion of an economic model. Fordism, the system of industrial mass production and mass consumption, rested on a class compromise (wages tied to productivity, a welfare state, strong trade unions), and this compromise sustained the liberal democratic institutions we now take for granted. What now looks like “the crisis of the German economy” is in fact the protracted crisis of this model. First, financialization and globalization shifted profits from production toward financial returns, and wages decoupled from productivity. The platform economy then intensified this, reshaping the public sphere and how economic and cultural value is distributed. German real wages have stagnated since the early 1990s, and low-skilled wages have fallen. Full-time wages in the East were 17 percent below Western levels in 2024. As Isabella Weber highlighted, 89 percent of AfD voters in Saxony-Anhalt fear they will be unable to pay their bills; food prices have risen 34.7 percent since 2021, while wages have risen only 14.8 percent. Germany is not alone. The real income of the middle of Hungary’s income distribution regained its 1980s level only in the late 2010s , and the real value of the average American wage has roughly stagnated since the 1980s. Both countries saw far-right parties take power. Wherever the industrial crisis is concentrated, the far right is consistently stronger. The crises of the eastern German states, northeastern Hungary, the American Midwest, or northern England are symptoms of one protracted crisis of the model. Yet in West Germany, too, the historic industrial powerhouse in the Ruhr region shows the same pattern: in Gelsenkirchen, held by the Social Democrats (SPD) without interruption since 1949, the AfD became the strongest party last year, and it records its highest results in the state’s old mining and steel towns. An economic shock is never merely economic. Saxony-Anhalt has lost a quarter of its population since reunification, and of 2.9 million people, 1.8 million will remain by 2040; the post-socialist transition in eastern Europe brought more than seven million excess deaths, and the American rust belt gave us the concept of deaths of despair . Long-term population decline is one of the strongest predictors of the AfD vote, just as Donald Trump is overrepresented in the counties with above-average mortality . Those who stay feel, with some justification, that they have been consigned to the scrap heap of history. Great economic transformations also intensify cultural tensions. Whoever loses their job also loses one of the foundations of their self-respect; along with industrial work, forms of knowledge, subcultures, and whole lifeworlds are devalued. In the competition for shrinking jobs and decaying public services, the immigrant is the easiest scapegoat: our own research shows that even perceived competition for health care increases hostility to immigration. In eastern Germany, too, anti-immigrant sentiment is a political product: the fewer the immigrants, the better it works. Across the “new federal states” in the former East Germany, the share of foreigners and the AfD vote are inversely related . Those whose economic and cultural capital this transformation devalued cannot make their voices heard in politics either. East Germans hold 12 percent of national leadership positions, one seat on the boards of the forty companies listed on the DAX stock exchange, and none among army generals. Among AfD voters, 83 percent believe that East Germans are second-class citizens , and two-thirds of Christian-Democrat and SPD voters think so too. Polanyi identified two systemic answers to the paralysis of democratic market economies. Besides the deadly embrace of fascism, the list also contained a second item, social democracy, which saved Scandinavia and the America of the New Deal from fascism. To the present systemic crisis, history has so far written only one answer, and Saxony-Anhalt shows what it looks like. As long as we read the crisis one variable at a time, nobody will offer the second answer.

articles.title: Securing Public Education’s Future w/ Cecily Myart-Cruz
articles.content: Block & Build is a weekly newsmagazine podcast from Convergence Magazine that examines the balance of political forces in the US from a movement perspective. Every week, host Cayden Mak explores what's… Leading a union can be difficult. Even more difficult? Leading the educators union in the second-largest school district in the country, United Teachers Los Angeles , through the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic. Today, we talk to the woman who did just that: immediate Past President of UTLA, Cecily Myart-Cruz. She was also the first woman of color to be elected to the position. During her tenure, she made strides in racial justice and protections for immigrants. She helped secure more financial protections for the district, its workers, and more. Under her leadership, UTLA was able to expand what is possible through organizing that includes the community, not just its members. But now, public schools across the country are under attack from the right, including the Trump Administration’s plans to dismantle the Department of Education. As she steps away from the position, she joins us to talk about her tenure from the start of the COVID-19 pandemic to her transition to a new role as a member of the National Education Association’s Executive Committee. We’ll also discuss the threats currently facing public education–a foundational piece of our democracy–everywhere.

articles.title: WFTU Statement on the 26th of July 2026 On the 73rd Anniversary of the Attack on the Moncada Barracks
articles.author: admin
articles.content: The World Federation of Trade Unions (WFTU) salutes the heroic Cuban people on the occasion of the 73rd anniversary of the attack on the Moncada Barracks. The 26th of July remains a historic milestone in the struggle of the peoples against exploitation and imperialist domination. The heroic action led by Fidel Castro and his comrades in Santiago de Cuba marked the beginning of the revolutionary process that culminated in the triumph of the Cuban Revolution and inspired generations of workers and peoples throughout the world. The ideals of sovereignty, social justice, internationalism and workers’ dignity that emerged from Moncada continue to illuminate the struggles of the international working class today. This year’s anniversary takes place under conditions of intensified imperialist aggression against Cuba. The criminal economic, commercial and financial blockade imposed by the United States continues to suffocate the Cuban economy and deliberately creates enormous difficulties for the Cuban people. The continued inclusion of Cuba on the arbitrary list of countries allegedly sponsoring terrorism further strengthens this unjust policy, restricting access to fuel, medicines, food, technology and essential resources, while attempting to isolate socialist Cuba internationally. Despite these unprecedented pressures, the Cuban working class and people continue to defend with dignity the achievements of their Revolution. Their resistance once again demonstrates that no blockade, no sanctions and no imperialist intervention can break the determination of a people committed to their sovereign right to determine their own future. The WFTU reiterates that Cuba is not alone! The WFTU has already called upon its affiliates and friends to continue and intensify practical solidarity initiatives, including humanitarian assistance and material support for Cuban workers facing the serious consequences of the blockade. International solidarity must be expressed not only through declarations but through concrete actions that strengthen the resilience of the Cuban people in the face of imperialist aggression. At the same time, the international class-oriented trade union movement stands firmly alongside Cuban workers. Inspired by the unanimous decisions of the WFTU Presidential Council, our affiliates throughout the world continue to strengthen the Global Campaign for Signature Collection, “Cuba is not alone! – FIRMO POR CUBA,” expanding solidarity in every workplace, every sector, every university and every community. The WFTU also renews its demand for the immediate and unconditional end of the criminal blockade against Cuba, the removal of Cuba from the list of state sponsors of terrorism, and the return of Guantánamo to the Cuban people. These are indispensable conditions for respecting international law, national sovereignty and the right of every people to freely choose its own political and social system. On this historic anniversary, the WFTU pays tribute to all those who sacrificed their lives for the Cuban Revolution and expresses its profound admiration for the enduring example of revolutionary Cuba. An example of solidarity, peace, social progress and internationalism that continues to inspire workers and peoples struggling against exploitation, war and imperialism across the globe. The voice of the international class-oriented trade union movement will continue to be heard in every continent: Hands off Cuba! End the blockade now! Cuba is not alone! ¡Viva el 26 de Julio!
